name: Hard Fork
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: When the Chain Splits: Hard Forks and the Politics of Upgrading a Blockchain
lesson.summary: A hard fork is a backward incompatible protocol change that forces every participant to upgrade or be stranded on a separate chain, turning a routine software update into a high stakes political event.
lesson.body:
A hard fork is a change to a blockchain's rules that makes previously invalid blocks valid, or previously valid blocks invalid, in a way old software cannot process. Because the new rules are not backward compatible, a node that does not upgrade rejects blocks produced under the new rules, and a node that does upgrade rejects blocks produced under the old rules. If every participant adopts the new software, the chain simply continues with no visible split. If adoption is not universal, the network permanently divides into two chains that share an identical history up to the fork block and diverge afterward, each with its own coins, its own balances, and its own community.

Hard forks happen for ordinary engineering reasons: fixing a critical bug, adding a wanted feature, or adjusting an economic parameter such as issuance or block size. What makes them different from an update to a normal piece of software is that a blockchain has no central authority who can push a change to everyone. As the governance chapter established, blockchains coordinate through rough consensus among miners or validators, node operators, exchanges, wallet developers, and users, none of whom can be compelled to upgrade. A hard fork is therefore not purely technical. It is a referendum: enough of the network has to voluntarily agree the new rules are the legitimate rules.

The clearest illustration is the 2016 split between Ethereum and Ethereum Classic. An attacker exploited a flaw in a smart contract called The DAO and drained roughly 3.6 million ether into a child account. Because part of Ethereum's stated philosophy held that code is the final word, reversing the theft required rewriting history, something many participants considered a betrayal of immutability. The majority hard forked to move the stolen funds to a recovery contract, creating the chain now called Ethereum. A minority refused and kept running the original, unaltered rules, preserving that chain as Ethereum Classic. Both chains still exist today, each claiming a legitimate reading of what the network was meant to be.

Bitcoin Cash tells a similar story with a different cause. Years of disagreement over how to scale Bitcoin, essentially whether to keep blocks small and route more activity off chain, or raise the block size limit to fit more transactions directly on chain, split the community in 2017. Supporters of bigger blocks hard forked away from Bitcoin, raising the block size to 8 megabytes and keeping the ticker BCH. The disagreement was not really about code; it was about which tradeoff between transaction throughput and the cost of running a full node the community valued more, a tension the ATAM chapters ahead will formalize as a tradeoff point.

A hard fork that splits the network also creates a subtle danger called a replay attack: a transaction broadcast on one chain can be valid on the other chain too, since both share the same transaction format and history up to the split. Developers who anticipate a contentious fork add replay protection, such as a distinct chain identifier or a modified signature format, so a transaction meant for one chain cannot be rebroadcast on the other. Bitcoin Cash added a new signature hash flag for exactly this reason; Ethereum Classic's early lack of replay protection caused real losses for users who assumed the two chains would stay separate automatically.
